comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
Interesting experiment. A few observations based on the numbers you shared:  
•  Starting balance 1000 → Final 386.77 (roughly -61% over \~6 months)  
•  Total trade volume: \~633k USDT  
•  Average stake \~84 USDT  
•  Timeframe: 1m  
•  Stoploss: -100%  
•  Max open trades: 1  
That is an extremely high turnover relative to capital. On a 1-minute timeframe with that volume, even a modest per-trade cost (spread + fees + slippage) will dominate almost any small edge. Rough order-of-magnitude: if effective round-trip cost is only 5–8 basis points, the strategy already needs a consistently positive expectancy larger than that just to break even. Most retail-style 1m strategies do not clear that bar after realistic costs.  
A few things that are hard to judge from the screenshot alone:  
1.  Were commissions, spreads, and slippage included in the backtest? On 1m with high turnover this is usually the decisive factor.  
2.  Was there any form of walk-forward / out-of-sample protection, or was the logic optimized on the same period it was tested?  
3.  What was the actual edge before costs (average win/loss, win rate, expectancy per trade)? The final PnL alone does not tell us whether the signal was slightly positive and then destroyed by costs, or already negative.  
In rigorous testing, a large fraction of strategies that look “interesting” on paper die once realistic execution costs and proper out-of-sample validation are applied. High-frequency / high-turnover approaches are especially sensitive to this. If the goal is to find something that survives real costs rather than just generate activity, it is usually more productive to measure the gross edge first, then subtract measured costs, and only then look at net expectancy.  
Happy to discuss methodology if useful. What was the approximate number of trades and the average gross return per trade before fees/slippage

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
A few things that are worth watching as the agent iterates:  
•  Improving win rate from 18% → 43% in a short time on the same period is common when the process is allowed to adapt to the data it is being tested on. The risk is that a large part of that improvement is fitting noise rather than capturing a stable edge.  
•  On 1-minute data with high turnover, even a 43% win rate can still be strongly negative after realistic costs, depending on the average winner/loser ratio. Win rate by itself does not tell you much without the payoff asymmetry and the actual cost per trade.  
•  “After a few hours of research and backtesting” is usually not enough time for a proper out-of-sample check. If the agent keeps adjusting the logic on the same historical window, the results will keep looking better while the real (unseen) performance stays weak or negative.  
A more reliable way to separate signal from fitting is:  
1.  Freeze the logic at some point.  
2.  Test it on a period the agent has never seen (or a properly purged walk-forward).  
3.  Measure gross expectancy first, then subtract measured costs (spread + fees + slippage).  
4.  Only then look at net result.  
If the win rate and expectancy hold up under those conditions, it is more interesting. Otherwise the improvements are mostly coming from optimization on the in-sample data.  
Happy to look at the numbers once you have a version that was not further adjusted after the test period was fixed

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Nice that you posted the bad results as well as the plan. The final balance in that run looks well below the start, and most of the strategies lost, so I'd treat it as a first test and not a verdict. Before changing the rules, I'd check that fees and slippage are in, since 1-minute trading can lose a lot to those alone. I'd also rerun it on a different stretch of months, because one period can mislead either way. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and an option to hold out the last part of the history, if you want a second place to check results.

replies.body: yes right, this is just setup tests done by the AI it self without any proper strategy, now after 3 hours i m seeing good improvements after fees and not on 1 minute.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good that fees are in now and you moved off the 1-minute chart. One caution: improvements found after a few hours of tuning on the same stretch of data can be the strategy fitting that period. I'd test the new version on months you didn't use while changing it, and treat the improvement as real only if it holds up there.

comments.author: Individual-Quote-958
comments.body: Nice that you're paper trading first. On a one minute timeframe fees and spread usually decide everything, so I'd rerun it with realistic costs per fill before tweaking the strategy. Win rate can go up while the account still loses money if the losers are bigger, so I'd track average win vs average loss and max drawdown too. I'd also keep a chunk of data the agent never sees until the end, otherwise it tends to just fit the backtest.
